title: Matthew Charles was released under the First Step Act, not a Trump commutation
description_medium: Matthew Charles was returned to prison in 2018 after a judge reversed an earlier sentence reduction. His lawyers and advocates sought presidential clemency, but he was released in January 2019 after the First Step Act became law and he was resentenced to time served. The assigned name “Mathew G. Charles” remains unverified as the same person.
description_long:
Matthew Charles’s case drew national attention in 2018 after he was sent back to prison. Sentenced in 1996 to 35 years for drug and firearms offenses, he served 21 years before a sentence reduction let him out in 2016. A judge later determined that the reduction had been based on an incomplete record and ordered him to serve the remainder. Advocates, including his pro bono lawyer Shon Hopwood, petitioned for presidential clemency while also working for broader sentencing reform.

Charles’s release came through a different route: after Trump signed the First Step Act in December 2018, a federal court resentenced him to time served, and he left prison on January 3, 2019, the first person released under the law. The Justice Department’s Trump commutations list does not include him. The assigned record’s spelling, “Mathew G. Charles,” also does not match the public case name, Matthew Charles, so their identity cannot be confirmed from the available record.

corrected_wording.original: Commutes Sentence of Mathew G. Charles
corrected_wording.replacement: Matthew Charles was released under the First Step Act, not a Trump commutation
corrected_wording.reason: The public record does not support describing Matthew Charles as a recipient of a Trump commutation.

source_access_notes: Justice Department commutation list checked for the recipient; CBS News read for the sentence-reduction reversal and clemency advocacy; Georgetown Law read for First Step Act resentencing and release.
blockers: The assigned name “Mathew G. Charles” does not match the public case name “Matthew Charles,” and no DOJ commutation entry confirms a presidential grant to either spelling.
rationale: The named commutation is unsupported: the DOJ list has no Matthew Charles entry, and contemporary reporting says his release followed First Step Act resentencing. The assigned middle initial/name differs from that public case name, so identity remains uncertain.

title: Trump pardons Michael Anthony Tedesco after an earlier pardon omitted a conviction
description_medium: Trump issued Michael Anthony Tedesco a full pardon on July 29, 2019. Tedesco had served 12 months in prison for a 1990 conviction involving cocaine and marijuana distribution. The White House said Barack Obama had pardoned him in 2017, but a clerical error left out the fraud conviction; Trump’s grant corrected that omission and restored eligibility for state licenses for Tedesco’s car-warranty business.
description_long:
Michael Anthony Tedesco’s 2019 pardon dealt with a gap in an earlier clemency grant. In 1990, he was convicted in Pennsylvania of drug-trafficking and fraud offenses tied to what the White House described as minor involvement in a drug crime. He accepted responsibility and pleaded guilty; the Justice Department lists a 12-month prison term and five years of supervised release. President Barack Obama pardoned Tedesco in 2017, but the White House said a clerical error meant that the pardon did not cover the fraud conviction.

On July 29, 2019, Trump issued a full and unconditional pardon covering the remaining conviction. The administration said the correction would make Tedesco eligible for state licenses needed to expand his car-warranty business. This was one of five pardons announced that day, all involving convictions more than two decades old. The chronology matters: Trump’s action completed relief left incomplete by the earlier grant, rather than pardoning a case that had never received clemency.
source_access_notes: White House July 29, 2019 statement read for the earlier Obama pardon, clerical omission, and licensing effect; DOJ table read for conviction and sentence; Reuters report read for the group of five recipients.
rationale: The administration’s contemporaneous statement explains the narrow purpose of the pardon: Obama’s 2017 grant omitted a fraud conviction, affecting state licensing for Tedesco’s business. DOJ corroborates the original case and sentence.

title: Trump pardons John Richard Bubala for 1990 conversion of government property
description_medium: Trump signed a full pardon for John Richard Bubala on July 29, 2019. Bubala had pleaded guilty in 1990 to improper use of federal property after transferring government automotive equipment to Milltown, Indiana, for municipal maintenance. The White House said he acted to help the town, sought no payment, and later volunteered with veterans and at funerals.
description_long:
John Richard Bubala received a full pardon on July 29, 2019, for a 1990 conviction involving government property. He had transferred automotive equipment belonging to the federal government to Milltown, Indiana, for use in town maintenance and pleaded guilty to its improper use. The White House described his aim as helping the town and said he sought neither payment nor recognition. The Justice Department lists his sentence as two years’ probation, including community and home confinement.

The administration’s explanation focused on Bubala’s public service after the case: he volunteered at a Veterans Affairs medical center, led classes about the American flag, and served on an honor detail for veterans’ funerals. The pardon was part of a July 2019 group of five grants to men with older convictions. The White House said the full pardons restored federal rights, including voting and firearm rights. The published rationale emphasized the local purpose it attributed to the original act and Bubala’s later charitable work.
source_access_notes: White House July 29, 2019 statement read for the property transfer and community-service account; DOJ table read for the case and sentence; Reuters report read for same-day context.
rationale: The White House describes the equipment transfer, Bubala’s stated purpose, and his later service; DOJ identifies the conviction and sentence. Both establish a July 29, 2019 full pardon.

title: Trump pardons Rodney Takumi after a 1987 illegal-gambling conviction
description_medium: Rodney M. Takumi received a full pardon from Trump on July 29, 2019, for a 1987 conviction involving participation in an illegal gambling business. The White House said Takumi was working at a gambling parlor when police raided it; he pleaded no contest and received two years’ probation and a $250 fine. He later ran a tax-preparation franchise within the Navajo Nation.
description_long:
Rodney M. Takumi’s pardon concerned a 1987 illegal-gambling case in Hawaii. The White House said Takumi was working at a gambling parlor when law enforcement raided it; he pleaded no contest and was sentenced to two years’ probation and a $250 fine. The Justice Department’s clemency table lists the same offense and sentence.

Trump granted Takumi a full pardon on July 29, 2019, alongside four other men with convictions dating from the 1980s and 1990s. The administration’s statement emphasized Takumi’s later work as a tax preparer and his ownership of a tax-preparation franchise within the Navajo Nation, describing him as generous and respected in his community. The pardon ended the remaining federal consequences of the conviction and restored federal rights. The White House presented the grant as recognition of a long interval after the offense and a productive life afterward; it did not claim that the underlying conviction had been overturned.
source_access_notes: White House statement read for Takumi’s arrest, plea, and subsequent work; DOJ table read for offense and sentence; Reuters read for the July 2019 group pardon context.
rationale: The clemency statement and DOJ list independently confirm the offense, disposition, sentence and July 2019 pardon; the White House provides Takumi-specific context about work after the case.

title: Trump posthumously pardons suffragist Susan B. Anthony
description_medium: On August 18, 2020, Trump posthumously pardoned Susan B. Anthony for her 1873 conviction after voting in Rochester, New York, when women could not legally vote. The grant coincided with the centennial of the 19th Amendment. Anthony had refused to pay her $100 fine. Historians and the museum bearing her name objected that she had regarded the conviction as a symbol of injustice.
description_long:
Susan B. Anthony cast a ballot in Rochester, New York, in 1872, nearly fifty years before the 19th Amendment secured women’s voting rights. A judge directed a guilty verdict in her 1873 trial for illegal voting and fined her $100; Anthony refused to pay. Trump issued a posthumous full pardon on August 18, 2020, at a White House event marking the amendment’s centennial. The administration presented the grant as recognition of Anthony’s suffrage work and a wrongful conviction.

The gesture was not universally welcomed. The National Susan B. Anthony Museum & House said it had not been consulted, and its director said Anthony would have opposed a pardon because she treated the conviction as proof of how authorities denied women the vote. Historians also debated how to represent Anthony’s legacy, including her conflicts over Black men’s voting rights. The pardon thus joined a commemorative milestone to a disagreement about whether clearing the conviction honored Anthony or weakened the political meaning she had attached to it.
source_access_notes: White House pardon statement read for the official account and rationale; DOJ clemency table read for the conviction and fine; Washington Post read for the centennial, Anthony’s refusal to pay, and contemporary objections from historians and the museum.
rationale: The White House gives the stated rationale; the Washington Post reports historians’ objection that Anthony considered the conviction a symbol and would have opposed the pardon. The DOJ list supplies the sentence.
